name: Carbon Tax
description: A direct price on greenhouse gas emissions, typically CO2 or CO2e. Applied upstream (fuel extraction), midstream (fuel import/distribution), or downstream (emitters). Provides price certainty but not quantity certainty.
examples: Canada federal carbon price ($65 CAD/tCO2 in 2024, rising to $170 by 2030)
Sweden carbon tax ($137 USD/tCO2, world's highest)
Chile carbon tax ($5/tCO2, covers ~40% of emissions)
Singapore carbon tax ($25 SGD/tCO2, rising to $50-80 by 2030)
political_economy_notes: Distributionally regressive without rebates. Visible price signal can trigger backlash. Revenue recycling critical for public acceptance.
interactions: ETS (can coexist as carbon price floor)

name: Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS / Cap-and-Trade)
description: Sets a quantitative cap on total emissions from covered entities. Entities trade permits. Provides emissions certainty but price uncertainty. Price discovery through market.
examples: EU ETS (world's largest, ~40% EU emissions, €65/tCO2 2024)
California-Quebec linked cap-and-trade (~$30/tCO2)
China national ETS (power sector only, ~$11/tCO2 CNY equivalent)
UK ETS (~£35/tCO2 post-Brexit)
RGGI (US Northeast power sector)
emission_reduction_effectiveness: Guaranteed reduction to cap level; market determines cost-effective abatement
political_economy_notes: Free allocation reduces competitiveness concerns but weakens incentive. Price volatility can undermine investment signals.

name: Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM)
description: Applies a carbon price to imported goods equivalent to what domestic producers pay under an ETS or carbon tax. Prevents carbon leakage and competitive disadvantage.
examples: EU CBAM (launched Oct 2023, full implementation 2026, covers steel/cement/aluminium/fertilisers/electricity/hydrogen)
Proposed US Clean Competition Act
UK exploring CBAM by 2027

typical_parameters.covered_goods: carbon-intensive traded goods (steel, cement, aluminium typically)
typical_parameters.verification: requires production carbon intensity data from exporters
typical_parameters.wto_compatibility: disputed — GATT Article XX environmental exception potential defense

emission_reduction_effectiveness: Reduces carbon leakage by 20-50% for covered sectors. Indirect pressure on trading partners to price carbon.
political_economy_notes: Significant diplomatic friction with developing countries. WTO legal risk. Data collection burden.
interactions: free allocation (must phase out as CBAM phases in)

name: Renewable Energy Mandate / Portfolio Standard
description: Legal requirement for a specific percentage of energy/electricity to come from renewable sources by a specified year. May be technology-specific (solar, wind) or technology-neutral.
examples: UAE: 44% clean energy by 2050 (Masdar + DEWA projects)
EU: 45% renewable electricity by 2030 (revised RED III)
US state RPSs: California 100% clean by 2045
India: 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030
Abu Dhabi Noor Energy: 1177 MW CSP + 100 MW solar PV
emission_reduction_effectiveness: Each percentage point of grid decarbonisation reduces electricity sector intensity proportionally
political_economy_notes: Technology cost reductions have made renewables mandates increasingly cost-neutral or beneficial. Grid stability costs (storage, backup) are additional.

name: Methane Emission Regulation
description: Direct regulations on methane emissions from oil & gas, coal, and agriculture sectors. Includes leak detection and repair (LDAR), limits on venting/flaring, and equipment standards.
examples: US EPA Subpart W (oil & gas methane reporting)
EU Methane Regulation 2024 (LDAR requirements for oil & gas)
Global Methane Pledge (30% reduction by 2030, 150+ countries)
IEA Net Zero: no new methane from fossil fuels by 2030

typical_parameters.flaring_limits: routine flaring zero by 2030 (World Bank pledge)
typical_parameters.coverage: well sites, gathering, processing, transmission, storage

emission_reduction_effectiveness: 30% methane reduction = ~0.3°C avoided warming by 2040 (near-term climate benefit). Typical cost: $0-10/tCO2e (often cost-negative via gas capture value).
political_economy_notes: Often cost-effective due to captured gas value. Oil & gas industry prefers voluntary programs. International coordination essential for global impact.
interactions: oil & gas revenue (captured gas has value)

name: Energy Efficiency Standard
description: Minimum performance requirements for energy-consuming equipment, vehicles, or buildings. Technology-forcing standards that reduce energy demand.
examples: EU ETS Buildings/Transport (ETS2 from 2027)
US CAFE standards (vehicle fuel economy)
UAE Green Building Code (Estidama Pearl Rating)
China vehicle efficiency standards (5.0 L/100km fleet average)
EU Ecodesign Regulation (appliances, lighting)
emission_reduction_effectiveness: Buildings efficiency: 30-60% energy savings potential. Vehicle standards: 15-40% fleet efficiency improvement over 10 years.
political_economy_notes: Well-accepted by public; reduces energy bills. Industry opposition to upfront costs. Technology lock-in risk if standards not regularly updated.
